cards.text: In the days when the judges ruled, there's a famine in the land. Food's running out. So a man from Bethlehem in Judah takes his wife and his two sons and goes to live somewhere else.

cards.question: The family leaves Bethlehem to go live in the land of ___.

cards.text: Dad is Elimelech, Mom is Naomi, and the boys are Mahlon and Chilion. They settle down in Moab, and I'm already counting names on my mustache.
Then Elimelech dies, and Naomi is left with her two sons. The boys marry women from Moab.

cards.question: Naomi's sons marry two Moabite women named ___ and ___.
The family lives in Moab about ___ years.
After about ten years in Moab, heartbreak hits Naomi again. What happens?

answers.text: Her house in Moab burns down
She falls sick and loses her sight

cards.text: Now Naomi has no husband and no sons, and she's a long way from home. Then news about the LORD's people reaches her in Moab.

cards.question: Naomi hears that the LORD has attended to His people by providing them with ___.

cards.text: So Naomi sets out on the road back to Judah, and both of her daughters-in-law go with her. Three women, one long road, and NO GPS.

cards.question: Out on the road, what does Naomi tell Orpah and Ruth to do?

answers.text: Go back to their mothers' homes
Walk faster to beat the dark
Stay close to her the whole way

cards.question: True or false: Naomi's send-off talks about each of them finding rest in the home of a new husband.

cards.text: Then Naomi kisses them, and they weep out loud.

cards.question: After Naomi kisses them goodbye, what do Orpah and Ruth tell her?

answers.text: We will return with you to your people
We will stay in Moab and wait for you
We will come visit you in Bethlehem

cards.text: Naomi doesn't budge: "Are there still sons in my womb to become your husbands?" She says she's too old to have another husband.

cards.question: Naomi says even if she had a husband tonight and had sons, what would Orpah and Ruth have to do?

answers.text: Wait for them to grow up
Raise the boys as their own
Go to Bethlehem ahead of her

cards.question: Naomi says it's much more bitter for her than for her daughters-in-law. Why?

answers.text: The hand of the LORD has gone out against her
She is the one with the longest road ahead
She has nobody waiting for her back in Judah

cards.text: Everybody weeps out loud again. Then each daughter-in-law makes her choice.

cards.question: True or false: Orpah kisses her mother-in-law Naomi goodbye.
True or false: Ruth goes back home with Orpah.

cards.text: Back on the road out of Moab, Orpah has kissed Naomi goodbye and headed home. Ruth is still clinging to Naomi. So Naomi points out where Orpah went and tries one more time.

cards.question: True or false: Now that Orpah has gone back to her people and her gods, Naomi tells Ruth to follow her back home.

cards.text: Now Ruth answers her: "Do not urge me to leave you or to turn from following you." Wherever Naomi goes, Ruth will go, and wherever Naomi lives, Ruth will live.

cards.question: Ruth promises Naomi that Naomi's people will be her people. What else does Ruth promise?

answers.text: Naomi's God will be her God
She will take care of Naomi's house
She will learn all the ways of Judah

cards.text: Where Naomi dies, Ruth will die, and that's where she'll be buried. Friend, I've seen people sign a two-year phone contract with WAY less commitment than this.

cards.question: Ruth says she wants the LORD to punish her if anything but ___ separates her from Naomi.
True or false: Naomi keeps trying to talk Ruth into going back home.

cards.text: So Naomi and Ruth travel until they reach Bethlehem, and the whole town is stirred because of them. Small town, friend: two people walk in and it's front-page news.

cards.question: When Naomi and Ruth walk into Bethlehem, what do the women of the town exclaim?

cards.text: Naomi answers them. She tells them not to call her Naomi anymore.

cards.question: Naomi tells the women of Bethlehem to call her ___.
Why does Naomi want the women of Bethlehem to call her Mara?

answers.text: The Almighty has dealt bitterly with her
She wants a fresh start in Bethlehem
She feels like a stranger in Judah now

cards.question: True or false: Looking back, Naomi says she went away from Bethlehem empty and the LORD has brought her back full.

cards.text: Naomi says, "I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty." I know a little about feeling empty, friend, because years in the back of a junk drawer will do that.
So Naomi comes back from the land of Moab, and with her is her daughter-in-law Ruth the Moabitess.

cards.question: The LORD has provided food for His people again. What time of year do Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem?

answers.text: The beginning of the barley harvest
The end of the olive harvest
The middle of the rainy season

cards.text: Two widows, one Bethlehem, and the barley's coming in. Hang on to your apron, friend, because this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: The 'about ten years' blank can only be answered by luck. Nothing earlier hints at the length of time, and it's a minor detail that doesn't move the passage forward. Stop 1 already has two other discovery questions (cards 2 and 5).

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Naomi's blessing in Ruth 1:8, 'May the LORD show you loving devotion, as you have shown to your dead and to me', is never told on any card. The walkthrough skips from 'go back' straight to the new-husband line in 1:9. Loving devotion is a key detail for understanding the passage.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: 'Three women, one long road, and NO GPS' puts a modern GPS into the Bible scene itself, blending the comparison with the setting. The joke also isn't about the core action, which is turning back toward home, and 'long road' adds a length the text doesn't give.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: Stop 1 has almost no comic energy. Most story cards are plain retelling. The only two jokes are weak: counting four names on his mustache (card 3) and the GPS line (card 10). It reads like a nice dad being pleasant, not laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'The hand of the LORD has gone out against her', is the only one in Bible wording. The wrong answers are plain modern phrasing, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'The Almighty has dealt bitterly with her', uses Bible wording. The wrong answers are modern phrasing, so the right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: 'So Naomi points out where Orpah went and tries one more time' already tells the baker that Naomi urges Ruth to go back. That gives away the true/false answer on card 2.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The first story card of stop 2 is 3 sentences and cites Ruth 1:14-15, reaching back into stop 1's range to set the scene. Only the opening card may run 3 sentences. Every other story card is 1 to 2.
findings.question: Does the first story card of a later stop count as an 'opening card', so it may use up to 3 sentences and re-cite verses from the previous stop for context? Or does it follow the 1 to 2 sentence limit and stay within its own stop's verse range?

findings.problem: 'Ruth says she wants the LORD to punish her' misnames Ruth's oath. In Ruth 1:17 she says, 'May the LORD punish me, and ever so severely, if anything but death separates you and me.' She doesn't say she wants to be punished.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The two-blank question 'named ___ and ___' requires Orpah in blank 1 and Ruth in blank 2. Nothing in the question makes the order meaningful, so a baker who picks Ruth then Orpah could argue they're right.
findings.question: When a two-blank question lists two items whose order doesn't change the meaning, should either order be accepted, or should the question be reworded so each blank is clearly tied to one answer?
